extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Plato; philosophers; general readers interested in rhetoric, ethics, and political theory
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt of Plato's Gorgias (Socratic dialogue) debating the nature of the good, the aims of rhetoric, the proper ends of arts and statesmanship, and the relationship between order in body and soul. The text articulates normative standards for rhetoric, education, rulers, and moral training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good soul = harmony and order
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul in which there is harmony and order is the good soul; the effect of harmony and order in the soul is 'lawful' action which produces temperance and justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates' body/soul analogy: just as health/strength name bodily order, 'lawful' names the regular order of the soul, yielding temperance and justice. Use this as the basic criterion for evaluating moral states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorician's proper aim: implant virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: A true and honest rhetorician will have his eye fixed upon implanting justice and temperance in the souls of citizens and taking away injustice and intemperance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with rhetoricians who flatter: the genuine rhetorician addresses souls with the aim of moral improvement (implanting every virtue and removing every vice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure is not identical with the good
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasant is not the same as the good; the pleasant should be pursued for the sake of the good, not for its own sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates uses this to refute pursuing indulgence as the highest aim; evaluative judgments must privilege the good over mere pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue arises from order, truth, and art
rubrics_metrics.description: The virtue of each thing (body, soul, instrument) comes as the result of order and truth and art imparted to it; what makes a thing good is the proper order inhering in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'order/arrangement' and 'knowledge/art' as standards for judging whether something (or someone) is functioning well or is virtuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance as central virtue leading to others
rubrics_metrics.description: An orderly or temperate soul will necessarily be just, holy, and courageous, and thus will do well in all things and be happy and blessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperance is presented as the foundational quality whose presence signals wider moral competence; evaluate persons/policies by whether they cultivate temperance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chastisement/restraint better than indulgence for a sick soul
rubrics_metrics.description: When the soul is intemperate or 'sick', restraining or chastising its appetites is better for the soul than allowing unrestrained satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to medical treatment of the body: governing or educating requires restraint of harmful desires rather than simple gratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding suffering injustice requires power
rubrics_metrics.description: To escape suffering injustice a man must provide himself with power (or be the equal/companion of ruling power); mere will is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess defenses/political positions by whether they secure sufficient power to avert harms; example discussion of tyrant and companions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding doing injustice requires art and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent doing injustice is not achieved by will alone; it requires study, practice, and the possession of an art (moral skill/education).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the dialogue: moral behavior depends on cultivated skill/knowledge (art), not merely intention; evaluate moral competence by evidence of training and habituation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship is based on likeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man is most the friend of him who is most like to him; a tyrant's true friend will resemble and be submissive to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to predict political and social alliances: judge likely friends/associates by similarity in character and aims; warns against molding youth to be like unjust masters.

rubrics_metrics.name: True statesmanship judged by whether citizens improve
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine good statesman should make the citizens better (more just, gentle) rather than worse; measure a statesman's value by the moral condition of the people over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates uses historical examples (Pericles, Themistocles, Cimon, Miltiades) to show that apparent success (buildings, revenues) is not the same as moral improvement; evaluate rulers by civic virtue produced, not by material achievements alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed competence requires demonstrable practice and success
rubrics_metrics.description: Before undertaking public works or public roles one must have been taught, practiced, and shown success in the relevant art (e.g., built private houses, cured private patients).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates' building and physician examples: assess professional claims by asking for masters, prior successful instances, and demonstrable experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of arts: mistress arts vs servile purveyors
rubrics_metrics.description: There are higher arts (gymnastics, medicine) that should govern lesser ministerial arts (bakers, cooks, vintners); similarly, genuine educators/statesmen should govern purveyors of luxury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between arts that aim at real health/improvement and those that merely supply pleasure; evaluate educators/statesmen by whether they aim to be 'mistress' arts, not mere purveyors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saving life is not necessarily equivalent to improving the good
rubrics_metrics.description: Arts that save life (pilot, pleader) may preserve bodies but do not necessarily improve souls; deliverance from danger can be of no profit to a wicked person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate technical success in saving lives with moral betterment; value arts that improve the soul above those that merely avert physical harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two processes of training: pleasure-oriented flattery vs improvement-oriented discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of training: one that treats beings with a view to pleasure (vulgar flattery) and one that treats them with a view to the highest good (resistance of desires).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to evaluate education, rhetoric, and policy: prefer methods that aim at improvement and self-control, not mere gratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric and sophistry as potentially corrupting flattery
rubrics_metrics.description: Orators and sophists may function like purveyors of luxury—flattering desires rather than instilling true virtue—and thereby corrupt citizens and the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat rhetorical skill with suspicion unless it is grounded in knowledge of justice; evaluate teachers/orators by their actual moral effects on pupils and citizens.
